extracted.intended_audience: stakeholders in the FTC non-compete rulemaking (employers, workers, attorneys, state attorneys general, economists, and public commenters)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and explanation of the FTC's final rule on non-compete clauses, including the Commission's rationale for rulemaking vs. adjudication and the required regulatory economic analysis under section 22 of the FTC Act. Contains findings, responses to public comments, and methodological choices for estimating costs and benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of rulemaking versus adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission has the authority to make rules and regulations to carry out the FTC Act's prohibition on unfair methods of competition under sections 5 and 6(g), and agencies generally have discretion to choose between rulemaking and adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking is appropriate here because the prevalence of non-competes and the scale of harms across the economy make rulemaking more efficient than case-by-case adjudication. Rulemaking provides clearer, more accessible notice of the application of section 5, streamlines proof required for enforcement, saves resources relative to individual litigation, allows public comment on a complete regulatory scheme, and is beneficial when a vast amount of data must be compiled and analyzed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate-harms rationale for a national rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal harms from non-competes arise from their tendency to negatively affect competitive conditions in the aggregate rather than necessarily from single agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single non-compete may have limited effect, but many non-competes across a market produce net negative effects on matching, new firm formation, and innovation. Because harms are aggregate, individual case adjudication is less able to address them; a national rule can address systemic negative externalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation cost and barrier considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual litigation is costly and time-consuming, deterring many workers (especially hourly workers) from challenging non-competes; liquidated damages and fee-shifting increase the risk of challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical and comment evidence of five- and six-figure litigation costs, time-consuming appeals that can outlast the non-compete period, reputational harms, and workers' fear of litigation support the Commission's finding that litigation costs inhibit challenges and create in terrorem effects that chill worker mobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: In terrorem effect and lack of drafting penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts' willingness to reform or sever overbroad non-competes (rather than striking them) and the absence of penalties for drafting overbroad covenants produce an in terrorem effect on employees and competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If courts routinely modify overbroad covenants instead of invalidating them, employers have little incentive to draft narrowly; the threat of enforcement (even if unenforceable) restricts worker mobility and competition. Commenters and literature (e.g., Harvard Law Review discussion) document this dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of Sherman Act/private litigation for non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: Private Sherman Act litigation is an ineffectual response for most workers because proving harm to competition in relevant markets is resource-intensive and requires expert testimony; plaintiffs must show harm to competition as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 5 is more inclusive than the Sherman Act — it requires indicia of unfairness and tendency to negatively affect competitive conditions without separate market-power proof. For individual litigants, the evidentiary and expense burdens make Sherman Act suits impractical for addressing widespread non-compete harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public enforcement resource constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Public enforcers (FTC, State attorneys general) have limited resources and cannot feasibly investigate or litigate every unlawful non-compete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FTC workforce limitations and competing priorities mean case-by-case public enforcement is unlikely to address the large volume of non-competes (the Commission estimates millions of firms and tens of millions of non-competes). A rule provides broader reach and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual litigation cannot remedy negative externalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonableness tests in individual non-compete cases typically consider employer interest, worker harm, and public injury from loss of services but do not account for harms to other workers, firms, consumers, and the broader economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many harms arise from aggregate use of non-competes, individual case assessments under State law or antitrust law often miss broader market effects; hence, case-by-case litigation is insufficient to redress systemic negative externalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of State law and need for a uniform standard
rubrics_metrics.description: State-by-state adjudication creates a patchwork of rules—choice-of-law clauses, forum-selection clauses, arbitration clauses, variable definitions of legitimate business interest, and differing approaches to reformation—that produce complexity, unpredictability, and opportunities to evade protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remote/hybrid work, cross-border employers and workers, and forum shopping can undermine State protections; choice-of-law and arbitration clauses can defeat local bans. A federal rule alleviates confusion, spillovers, and incentives for permissive State policies to attract employers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of State experimentation is limited here
rubrics_metrics.description: Although States have enacted varied non-compete laws and serve as laboratories, the Commission finds that a century of State experimentation has already generated extensive empirical evidence showing negative aggregate effects of non-competes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission disagrees that further State 'laboratory' testing is needed given the body of empirical research; a uniform rule would improve competitive conditions nationwide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 22 regulatory analysis requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 22 of the FTC Act directs the Commission to issue a final regulatory analysis that analyzes projected benefits and any adverse economic effects and summarizes significant issues raised by comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preliminary regulatory analysis must contain: (1) a concise description of the need for, and objectives of, the proposed rule; (2) a description of any reasonable alternatives to the proposed rule that may accomplish the objective consistent with law; and (3) for the proposed rule and each alternative, a preliminary analysis of projected benefits and adverse effects. The final analysis must quantify where possible and discuss data sources, assumptions, and uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantification, data sourcing, baseline, and uncertainty disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: For quantified benefits and costs, the analysis must identify data sources relied upon, quantitative assumptions made, and measure effects against a baseline where no rule is promulgated; discuss bases for uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some effects may be quantifiable but not monetizable; others may be unquantifiable. The Commission should conduct sensitivity analyses and be transparent about assumptions; failure to monetize does not undermine conclusions if appropriately discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological approaches and sensitivity analysis for earnings/innovation estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission should use multiple estimation approaches (including approaches that avoid extrapolation) and sensitivity analyses to test robustness of conclusions about earnings, innovation, and other effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final analysis adopts an 'average enforceability change approach' (assuming historical average State-level enforceability change represents total change) and also conducts sensitivity analyses with linear extrapolation approaches to scale literature estimates toward a near-comprehensive ban. Use of multiple methods helps address extrapolation concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish transfers from net benefits and focus on economic surplus
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analysis should focus on net benefits to society (economic surplus), not nominal changes in dollar output; some items (e.g., tax consequences) may be transfers rather than net social gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, tax ramifications from non-compete changes may represent transfers from government to firms; the Commission also preserved existing non-competes for senior executives to mitigate tax-administration burdens. Analysis should explicitly account for transfers vs. efficiency gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope exclusions for regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs related to litigation over the validity of the rule are outside the scope of section 22 regulatory analysis, which addresses costs and benefits should the final rule be implemented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis need not quantify potential costs of future constitutional or validity challenges; it should concentrate on the effects of implementation rather than pre- or post-implementation litigation over the rule's validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization limits for innovation and appropriate proxies
rubrics_metrics.description: Patenting activity can be used as a proxy for innovation, but patenting does not capture the full social value of innovation and the social value of patents is difficult to monetize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission can use patenting as an imperfect proxy and may stop short of monetizing social value where estimates are unavailable; empirical literature suggests increased innovation following decreased enforceability is not merely substitution into patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of training type (core vs advanced) and welfare implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses of training effects should consider whether observed increases in training under greater non-compete enforceability reflect core (baseline) training or advanced (productivity-enhancing) training, since decreases in core training may be economically beneficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because evidence does not reliably distinguish core from advanced training in the literature, the Commission treats decreased core training as a potential net benefit (greater labor efficiency) while recognizing that decreases in advanced training would be a net cost.
